original_title: An Analysis of Afghan Onward Movements from Iran to Türkiye
title: An Analysis of Afghan Onward Movements from Iran to Türkiye
original_summary:
Countries: Türkiye, Iran (Islamic Republic of)
Source: UN High Commissioner for Refugees

Please refer to the attached file.

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
This report examines protection risks along the
South-West Asia route, living conditions, and
drivers of onward movement among Afghans who
transited through the Islamic Republic of Iran
before travelling onward to Türkiye. It is based on
855 interviews conducted in Türkiye between late
December 2025 and January 2026 and forms
part of a route based approach to analyzing risks
and decision making along the Iran–Türkiye
segment of the South-West Asia route.
The findings should be interpreted in the context
of a rapidly evolving regional environment. Since
data collection, a sharp escalation of hostilities in
the Middle East beginning on 28 February 2026
has significantly affected the political, security and
socioeconomic environment in Iran and
neighbouring countries. These developments
have led to increased security measures,
economic disruption and tighter restrictions on
movement. While the findings reflect conditions at
the end of 2025, they remain relevant for
understanding onward movement dynamics,
particularly where pressures may have intensified.
The analysis identifies two overlapping movement
patterns.
First, 30 per cent of Afghan respondents reported
that Iran was “just a transit country,” indicating no
intention to remain. This group is predominantly
male (approximately 75 per cent men and 25 per
cent women), reflecting a gendered pattern of
transit oriented movement.
Second, among those who did not consider Iran
solely as a transit country (70 per cent), onward
movement is primarily driven by conditions
experienced in Iran rather than pre-planned
intentions. Within this group, 95 per cent cited
legal uncertainty, discrimination, protection risks,
poor living conditions, and economic hardship as
key drivers.
Legal status constraints and discrimination are the
most consistent drivers, while protection and
socioeconomic pressures tend to accumulate
over time. Afghans who worked or remained in
Iran for extended periods often described onward
movement as a response to accumulating
constraints and risks, rather than part of their initial
plans.
Overall, the findings show that onward movement
from Iran cannot be explained by a single factor or
a simple transit versus destination dichotomy.
While a minority view Iran strictly as a transit point,
for many others, onward movement is gradual and
reactive, shaped by cumulative legal, protection
and livelihood pressures.

original_title: World: Aid in Danger Bi-Monthly News Brief (15-28 April 2026)
title: World: Aid in Danger Bi-Monthly News Brief (15-28 April 2026)
original_summary:
Countries: World, Democratic Republic of the Congo, Haiti, Lebanon, Myanmar, occupied Palestinian territory, South Sudan, Sudan, Ukraine
Source: Insecurity Insight

Please refer to the attached file.

Between 01 January and 31 March 2026, Insecurity Insight identified at least 66 incidents in which aid workers were killed, injured, kidnapped or arrested (KIKA). Across these incidents, 26 aid workers were killed, 61 injured, 17 kidnapped and 27 arrested. KIKA incidents occurred across 17 countries and territories and were particularly concentrated in South Sudan (14 incidents) and Iran (10 incidents).

82% of recorded health worker kidnappings took place in Mali’s Gao and Sikasso regions and in South Sudan’s Central Equatoria state, where protracted, high-intensity conflict continues to drive insecurity and elevated levels of harm to aid workers delivering life-saving assistance. In Iran, at least three aid workers were killed and 14 injured in U.S.-Israeli aircraft strikes between 02 March and 31 March.

Download the data (updated every Monday). Insecurity Insight continuously backdates data, as such, numbers may change if or when further information is made available.
